unit.title: Coordinate the installation of electrical wiring support system infrastructure

summary: This unit teaches you to plan, coordinate and check the installation of the systems that carry and protect electrical cables: cable tray, ladder and basket, trunking, conduit, strut channel and hangers. You will choose the right system and finish for the job and for Jamaica's climate, work out quantities and costs, agree routes with other trades, supervise a crew safely, bond and inspect the finished run, and keep the records.

blocks.p: Before any cable is pulled, something has to hold it up, route it and protect it. That something, the **wiring support system**, is cable tray, ladder, basket, trunking, conduit and the brackets, hangers and fixings that hold them. A poor support system sags, rusts, clashes with the air-conditioning ducts, or fails in a hurricane, and it is expensive to change once cables are in. At Level 3 you do not only fix it: you **coordinate** it. You read the drawings and specification, choose the system, work out the materials, agree routes with the other trades, brief and supervise the crew, check the work and keep the records. (Pulling cables and fixing light fittings are covered in MEMMRD0683A.)

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the work
Read the drawings and specification, survey the site, find clashes, take off quantities, order materials and plan the order of work.
Choose the system
Select tray, ladder, basket, trunking or conduit and its material and finish to suit the cables, the location and the climate.
Work out loads and sizes
Check cable weights against the tray's safe working load, support spacing, bend radius and trunking fill.
Coordinate with other trades
Compare drawings, agree routes, heights and clearances at coordination meetings and keep written minutes.
Choose fixings and supports
Pick anchors for concrete, hollow block and roofs; build trapeze hangers, brackets and frames correctly.
Protect against corrosion, heat and weather
Use hot-dip galvanised or stainless parts near the sea, UV-resistant PVC outdoors, expansion fittings and secure fixings for hurricanes.
Bond and segregate
Bond metal supports where specified, keep power and data apart, and fire-stop openings.
Work safely
Control work at height, drilling dust, manual handling and live services; use permits.
Supervise and inspect
Brief the crew, set out accurately, check quality, snag and sign off before cables are installed.
Keep records
Take off, cost, programme, minutes, as-built drawings and snag lists.

ul: Many buildings are made of **concrete and hollow concrete blocks**, with flat roofs and some open-sided structures. Fixings that hold in solid concrete may not hold in a hollow block's cores.
**Salt air** near the coast, strong **sun**, heavy **rain** and **hurricanes** shape every choice of material, finish and fixing.

Jamaica's code is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**, with US-style trade names (EMT, rigid conduit, cable tray, wireway). Specifications may also use British terms (trunking, ladder). This kit gives both.
Supply is **110/220 V, 50 Hz**. Heavy cables on tray are common in hotels, factories, hospitals and warehouses.

blocks.note: Never describe a particular supplier's product as 'best'. Select by the specification, the maker's data and the conditions of the job.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: At Level 3 you work from the specification, not from habit. You answer for the crew's safety, the quality of the finished run, the cost and the programme. Know when to raise a problem: a clash, a change, a defect or a delivery that does not match the order.

sections.title: Planning the work and working with other trades

head: Document
What you take from it
rows: Electrical drawings
Routes, tray and trunking sizes, risers, positions of boards and equipment
Specification
Type of system, material and finish, support spacings, fixings, space factor, bonding, fire-stopping, tests
Other trades' drawings
Ducts, pipes, sprinklers, structure, ceilings and lights that share the space
Makers' data
Safe working loads, bend radii, fixings and torque figures
Programme
Dates when areas are free and the order of the trades

blocks.p: Walk the route with the drawings. Look for beams, columns, ducts, pipes, sprinkler lines, existing services, low ceilings and access limits. A **clash** is where two services want the same space. Find clashes on paper, before the crew fixes anything, and raise them at the **coordination meeting**.

flow: Compare your drawings with the plumbing, air-conditioning, fire protection, ceiling and structural drawings
Mark every place where routes cross or crowd
Bring the clashes to the coordination meeting
Agree who goes where, at what height, with what clearance
Write it in minutes and on marked-up drawings; circulate them
Check on site that the agreement is followed; raise new problems at once

ul: Large ducts and drains that need a fall usually have priority, then cable tray, then smaller pipes. Agree this rather than assume it.
Keep cables **below** water pipes where possible, and away from hot pipes.
Leave **access** above and beside the tray for laying cables, heat release and later maintenance.
Tell the ceiling installer where access panels are needed.
Minutes record what was agreed, by whom and by when. Without them, trades argue later about what was said.

blocks.p: In a new building the support systems usually go in **after the structure is complete and before the ceilings close**, so the crew can reach the work, and cables can follow. Work such as core drilling through slabs and walls comes early. Cables are pulled only after the supports have been inspected.

When the architect moves a wall or another trade changes a route, do not carry on with the old route or invent a new one. **Get the change in writing**, update the drawings, tell the crew and recalculate quantities and cost. Record the extra work.

Work out how long a job will take from output rates. **Example:** a crew of 3 fits about 12 m of tray each per day. For 180 m: 180 ÷ (3 × 12) = 5 days. Allow for access equipment, deliveries and other trades. A simple bar chart (programme) shows tasks against dates, and is updated as work proceeds.

sections.title: Choosing the system and the materials

head: System
What it is
Best used for
rows: Cable ladder
Two side rails joined by rungs
Heavy power cables over long spans: factories, plant rooms, risers. Strong; heat escapes freely.
Perforated cable tray
Flat sheet with holes and turned-up sides
Medium and smaller cables; general use in plant rooms and ceiling spaces.
Cable basket (wire-mesh tray)
Welded steel wire
Light data and control cables over ceilings; quick to cut and shape; not for heavy power cables over long spans.
Trunking
A closed box with a lid, steel or PVC; may have dividers
Neat surface runs on walls in offices, classrooms and workshops; dividers keep power and data apart.
Conduit
A closed tube: PVC, steel (EMT or heavier rigid), or flexible
Best protection from damage and weather: in walls and concrete, outdoors, where cables could be knocked. Steel gives strength; PVC resists corrosion.
Strut (slotted) channel
A steel channel with slots
Not for carrying cables: it makes brackets, frames and trapeze hangers.

head: Material or finish
Where to use it
Notes
rows: Pre-galvanised steel (zinc coated before forming)
Indoors, dry areas
Cut edges are bare steel and need touching up with zinc-rich paint.
Hot-dip galvanised after making
Outdoors, damp or corrosive areas
Thick zinc coating, including on cut and drilled edges if cut before dipping.
Stainless steel
Near the sea, in kitchens, pool plant rooms, food factories
Best corrosion resistance; costs more. Use stainless fixings with it.
Aluminium
Light duty; some outdoor uses
Do not fix it directly to copper or brass in damp or salty air: it corrodes quickly (galvanic corrosion).
Plain mild steel, painted on site
Not for outdoors or damp places
Paint wears and rust starts at scratches.
PVC
Outdoors if **UV-resistant**; wet and corrosive areas
Ordinary PVC goes brittle in strong sun. It expands and contracts a lot with heat.
Fibreglass (GRP)
Highly corrosive places
Does not rust; heavier loads need checking against the maker's data.

head: Condition
Effect
What to do
rows: Salt air at the coast (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios, Kingston Harbour)
Rapid corrosion of plain or thinly coated steel, and of fixings
Hot-dip galvanised or stainless parts; stainless fixings; treat every cut edge; avoid mixing metals.
Strong sun
Ordinary plastics go brittle and fade
UV-resistant PVC and cable sheaths outdoors.
Heat
PVC expands: a 30 m run can lengthen by well over 10 mm with a 30 °C rise; steel expands less
Expansion couplings in long PVC runs, with saddles that let the conduit slide.
Heavy rain and humidity
Water enters boxes and conduit; condensation
Weatherproof boxes, glands and covers; drain holes where the maker allows; slope conduit so water does not run into boards.
Hurricanes
Wind loads and flying debris act on outdoor supports
Closer supports, anchors rated for the load, runs kept close to the building; inspect after storms.
Hollow block walls and flat concrete roofs
Fixings can fail in hollow cores; roof waterproofing can be damaged
Fixings suited to hollow block or through-bolts; free-standing roof blocks for roof runs.

blocks.p: PVC expands by about 0.06 mm per metre for each °C of temperature rise. A 30 m run that warms by 30 °C lengthens by about 30 × 30 × 0.06 = **54 mm**. If it cannot move, it buckles or pulls off its fixings. Fit **expansion couplings** at the intervals the maker gives, and fix the run with saddles that allow it to slide, anchoring only at one point between couplings.

blocks.h: Where each system is not suitable

ul: Cable basket carrying heavy power cables over long spans, or running outdoors in salt spray: it is light duty and its thin wires corrode.
Plain painted mild steel outdoors near the sea.
Plastic clips for large cables on a roof structure.
Flexible conduit left hanging loose as the fixed route.

blocks.p: Makers give a tray or ladder's **safe working load (SWL)**, usually in **kg per metre** (kg/m), for a stated support spacing. The weight of the cables on the run, and any extra such as a person's weight during installation, must be below it, with a margin. An overloaded tray sags, and its supports can fail. If you change the spacing, the SWL changes: closer supports allow a higher load.

**Example:** cables weigh 18 kg/m in total and the maker's SWL at the chosen spacing is 25 kg/m. Spare capacity is 25 − 18 = 7 kg/m, which allows for cables to be added later. If the cables weigh 30 kg/m and the supports are 1.5 m apart, **each support carries** 30 × 1.5 = 45 kg of cables (plus the tray's own weight).

Support spacings come from the **specification and the maker's data**, never from the installer's habit or the fewest brackets. Typical spacings for tray and ladder are about 1.5 m for light or medium loads, closer for heavy loads, and shorter at joints, bends and tees. Always put a support near each joint and near each bend.

head: Number of supports for a straight run of length L, spacing s, supports at both ends
Formula
Example: 60 m, 1.5 m
rows: Spans
L ÷ s
Supports
spans + 1
41, plus extra at bends

blocks.p: Trunking and conduit must not be crammed with cables: cables need room to be drawn in without damage, and to lose heat. The limit is the **space factor**: the percentage of the inside area that cables may fill. A common figure for trunking is **45%**, but use the one in the specification.

**Example.** Trunking 75 mm × 50 mm inside: area = 3 750 mm². At a 45% space factor, the largest total cable area allowed is 3 750 × 0.45 = **1 687.5 mm²**. Add up the cable areas (the overall area of each cable, from the maker's data) and compare. Do not add cables after the limit is reached. Leave room for future additions where the client asks for it.

ul: Every bend must suit the **minimum bending radius of the largest cable** on the run. A tight bend damages the cable. The cable maker gives the radius, often 6 to 12 times the cable diameter for large power cables.
Conduit with more than the allowed number of bends (usually the equivalent of two 90° bends between draw-in points) needs a **draw-in box**, so cables can be pulled in without damage.
Use tray fittings (bends, tees, risers) made for the tray, not folded or cut tray.

blocks.p: A **take-off** lists every item needed, read from the drawings, with an allowance for waste.
**Worked example.** A tray route is 52 m long. Tray comes in 3 m lengths at J$8 500 each. Allow 10% extra for waste.

ol: Lengths: 52 ÷ 3 = 17.3; allow 10%: 17.3 × 1.1 = 19.1, so order **20 lengths** (always round up).
Supports at 1.5 m: 52 ÷ 1.5 = 34.7, so 35 spans and **36 supports**. Brackets at J$1 400 each: 36 × 1 400 = J$50 400.
Anchors, 2 per support at J$140 each: 72 × 140 = J$10 080.
Total before GCT: 170 000 + 50 400 + 10 080 = **J$230 480**. GCT is added at the current rate.

blocks.p: Other costs not in the take-off: bends and fittings, fire-stopping, labour, access equipment, transport and the contractor's overhead. Always say what is **not** included in an estimate.

blocks.note: Round up when you order: 17.3 lengths means 18 or 19 whole lengths, never 17. Waste is never zero, and a second delivery costs time.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Background
Suitable fixings
Notes
rows: Solid concrete slab or beam
Mechanical expansion or wedge anchors, rated for the load; chemical (resin) anchors for heavy loads or near edges
Fit as the maker says: drill size, depth, cleaned hole, torque. Pull-test a sample where the specification asks.
Hollow concrete block
Anchors made for hollow block (sleeve or toggle types), or through-bolts, or fix at the solid joints
Ordinary expanding anchors may not grip in the hollow cores.
Solid block or masonry
Sleeve or screw anchors
Check the maker's data for the block type.
Steel structure
Beam clamps, or drill and bolt as the structural engineer allows
Never weld or drill structural steel without permission.
Timber
Coach screws or bolts of suitable size
Check the timber is sound.
Flat concrete roof
Free-standing roof blocks or supports approved for the roof
Never bolt through the waterproof membrane.

ul: Plastic plugs with wood screws, masonry nails and glue alone are **not** suitable for loaded supports.
Fixings are chosen for the **total load**, including the tray, the cables and a safety factor, and for wind, vibration or uplift where relevant.
Stainless or hot-dip galvanised fixings outdoors and near the sea.

blocks.p: A **trapeze hanger** is a length of strut channel hung from the ceiling slab by two threaded rods, carrying tray or conduit on top. It is a flexible way to support several runs at once.

flow: Mark the positions from the set-out and check for hidden services
Fit the threaded rods, cut to length
Fix the strut across the rods with nuts and washers, with a **lock nut or locking washer** above and below
Level the strut with a spirit level or laser
Fix the tray to the strut with clips or bolts

ul: Lock nuts or locking washers stop the nuts working loose from vibration.
Do not exceed the rod's or strut's rated load; the maker gives it for each span.
Cut ends of galvanised strut and rod need touching up with zinc-rich paint, and sharp edges filed smooth.

blocks.p: Set out accurately before fixing. Use a **laser level** (a rotating or line laser) to mark a long, level route, and a **chalk line** to snap a straight mark. Measure the bracket positions at the specified spacing from a datum, and have another person check them with a tape. Check the wall or slab with a **cable detector** for hidden cables and pipes before drilling.

ul: Cut with a hacksaw or pipe cutter and **ream or deburr** the ends so sharp edges do not cut cable insulation.
Bend steel conduit with a bender to the correct radius, without kinking. PVC may be bent with a spring or heat, as the maker says.
Fit saddles at the specified spacing; closer spacing at bends and outdoors; fit couplers, boxes and glands fully tight.
Allow for **expansion** in PVC runs, and for **drainage** outdoors.
Fit draw-in boxes or inspection fittings so that cables can be pulled in and removed later.

blocks.p: Metal tray, ladder, trunking and conduit can become live if a damaged cable touches them. Where the specification says to bond them, they are connected to the installation's **earth** so that a fault current can flow and the protective device trips quickly. Join each section to the next with the maker's couplers, or with **bonding links or straps** across joints, especially painted joints, expansion joints and flexible sections. Clean contact surfaces of paint and dirt, and use the right washers (star washers cut through coatings). Connect the system to the main earthing terminal or board earth bar with a conductor of the specified size.

**Test** the bonding with a **low-resistance ohmmeter**, with its leads **nulled**, and with nothing connected to any supply: measure from the earth bar to the far end of each run, and across joints. The readings should be very low and steady. Record them, and put right any high reading. Do not use an insulation tester or a voltage tester for this.

blocks.note: Metal tray is not used as the circuit's neutral or protective conductor unless the design allows. Bond it as the specification says.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Segregation** keeps power cables apart from data, communication and fire-alarm cables, so interference from the power cables does not affect signals, and a fault on one system does not damage another. Use separate tray, trunking with a divider, or the spacing the specification states. Do not tie them together, lay data cables on top of power cables, or run them in the same conduit.

Where cables or their supports pass through a **fire-rated wall or floor** (in hospitals, hotels, schools and offices), the opening must be sealed with an approved **fire-stopping system** (sealant, board, pillows or collars), used as the maker's tested method says. Do not leave a gap for 'air flow', do not pack it with offcuts and tape, and do not cover it with hardboard. Fire-stopping is checked and recorded, because it holds back fire and smoke so people can escape.

ul: Choose the finish for the location (see 'Choosing the system and the materials').
After cutting **hot-dip galvanised** tray, remove burrs and coat the cut end with **zinc-rich paint**. Do not leave bare steel, and do not wrap it in tape.
Avoid contact between aluminium and copper or brass in damp conditions; use isolating washers if the metals must meet.
Store galvanised tray **off the ground, covered and dry**: stacked wet, it can develop 'white rust'.
Check outdoor supports after every storm.
When materials arrive, check them against the order: type, size, finish, quantity and condition. Note any damage or shortage on the delivery note **before** signing.
Store tray, trunking and conduit flat, supported along their length, off the ground, covered and dry. Keep PVC out of strong sun.
Keep fixings and small parts in labelled boxes in a locked store, with a record of what is issued.

head: Access
Use it for
rows: Mobile scaffold tower with guard rails and locked wheels, or a MEWP (mobile elevating work platform, such as a scissor lift) used by trained people
Work several metres up, or for most of a day
Platform steps
Short, light tasks at modest height
Ladder
Access only, or a very short task, tied or footed; never a ladder leaning on tray
Not allowed
Chairs, boxes, pallets, tables, or standing on tray or frames

ul: Barrier off the area below the work, and use tool lanyards so nothing falls on people.
Never work alone at height. Check the equipment before each use.
Hurricane-season storms and lightning: stop work outdoors and at height when they threaten.

blocks.p: Drilling and cutting concrete and block produces silica dust, which damages lungs. Use **dust extraction** on the drill and a suitable **mask**, with eye and ear protection. Wetting the floor afterwards does not protect the lungs of the person drilling. Warn occupants and sweep with a vacuum, not a broom.

ul: Check the drawings and use a **cable detector** (and pipe locator) before drilling.

If the route passes **live** equipment, such as busbar trunking or existing boards, plan the work with a **permit to work**: the live equipment is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester proved before and after, or otherwise made safe as the permit says. Never work close to live parts 'carefully' without telling anyone.
Cover or barrier live parts that stay on, and keep tools and tray lengths clear of them.
Tray and ladder lengths are awkward: two people carry and lift them; use trolleys and hoists for heavy items.
Jamaica's heat causes heat stress: plan breaks in shade, drinking water and lighter tasks in the hottest hours.

blocks.p: Each morning give a short **work plan or toolbox talk**: the day's tasks and who does each, the areas, the materials and access equipment needed, and the hazards and controls. Include the agreed heights and routes. Check the first brackets of each new run before the crew carry on.

ul: Check the first items of each person against the drawings and specification: height, level, spacing, fixings, joints.
Correct problems at once and explain why; pair less experienced workers with experienced ones.

If a bracket spacing is wrong (for example 2.5 m where the specification says 1.5 m), have the extra brackets fitted **before** cables go in. Do not accept it because the tray is empty and looks fine.

blocks.p: If a run is fixed at the wrong height and will clash with a duct to come: stop work on that run, confirm the agreed height from the drawings and minutes, find out why without blame (old drawing, wrong mark, change not passed on), tell the other trade early, correct it before cables go in, record the time and materials, and stop it recurring by controlling drawings on site, setting out heights with a laser and checking each new run's first brackets.

At the end of each day compare progress with the plan, update the marked-up drawings and note problems such as clashes or late deliveries. Send the supervisor a short progress report: work done, problems, what is needed.

blocks.h: Inspecting a finished run before cables are pulled

head: Check
What to look for
rows: Route, height and clearances
As drawn and agreed; no clashes; space above and beside
Supports
Correct type, spacing, level and square; at joints and bends; fully tightened and locked
Fixings
Right type for the background, all in place, none loose; pull-tested where specified
Joints and couplers
Bolted, aligned, with no sharp edges or burrs
Bends and fittings
Suit the cable bending radius; draw-in boxes where needed
Bonding
Links fitted across joints; low-resistance test results recorded
Finishes
Right finish for the location; cut edges treated; no damage to coatings
PVC runs
UV-resistant; expansion couplings fitted; saddles let it slide
Fire-stopping and segregation
Planned or done where cables cross fire walls; separate routes or dividers for power and data
Cleanliness
No debris, swarf or offcuts inside the tray or conduit

ul: **Inspection checklist** for each run, with photographs of any defects.
**Snag list**: each defect, who will fix it and by when. Sign off only when all snags are cleared and rechecked.
**As-built drawings**: updated as the supports go in, so the owner knows where the routes really run. They are the owner's record for later work.
**Minutes** of coordination meetings and written confirmation of changes.
Delivery notes, test results of the bonding, and photographs, filed for the project.

blocks.note: As-builts are updated **as you go**, not at the end from memory. A drawing that does not show where the tray really runs causes damage and delay for the next contractor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Hand over the inspected, snag-free system to the cable crew or the main contractor with its drawings, test results and any maker's data. Tell them of limits such as the tray's SWL and spare capacity.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can read the drawings and specification and survey a site for clashes.
I can coordinate with other trades through a coordination meeting and write minutes.
I can describe the order of work for support systems in a new building.
I can handle a change in writing and update the drawings.
I can choose between ladder, tray, basket, trunking, conduit and strut for a job.
I can choose materials and finishes for Jamaican conditions, and treat cut edges.
I can allow for the expansion of PVC and use UV-resistant PVC outdoors.
I can check cable weight against safe working load and work out the load on a support.
I can work out the number of supports and the length of tray to order, with waste.
I can calculate the allowed cable area in trunking from the space factor.
I can estimate the cost of a run in J$ before GCT, and say what is not included.
I can choose fixings for solid concrete, hollow block and roofs.
I can build and check a trapeze hanger with lock nuts.
I can set out a route with a laser level and chalk line and check for hidden services.
I can explain why metal supports are bonded, and bond and test them with a nulled low-resistance ohmmeter.
I can keep power and data cables segregated and fire-stop openings in fire walls.
I can control work at height, dust, live services and manual handling.
I can brief and supervise a crew and deal with defective work.
I can inspect a finished run, keep a snag list and as-built drawings, and report progress.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: Supports = (length ÷ spacing) + 1
Number of supports on a straight run, plus extras at bends
Load per support = kg/m × spacing
Weight carried by one support
Allowed cable area = inside area × space factor
Trunking fill; 45% is a common figure
About 0.06 mm per metre per °C
Expansion of PVC
Order = length ÷ 3 m, + 10% waste, rounded up
Tray lengths to order
Crew output: days = length ÷ (people × metres per person per day)
Programme
Two lock nuts or locking washers
Stop threaded rod nuts working loose
Low-resistance ohmmeter, leads nulled
Instrument to test bonding

terms: As-built drawings
Drawings updated to show where the routes and supports were actually installed.
Bonding
Joining metal parts, such as tray sections, to earth so a fault current can trip the protective device.
Cable basket
Welded wire mesh tray for light data and control cables.
Cable ladder
Heavy-duty support with side rails and rungs, for long spans and heavy cables.
Clash
A place where two services want the same space.
Coordination meeting
The meeting where trades agree routes, order of work and clashes.
Draw-in box
A box in a conduit run where cables can be pulled in.
Expansion coupling
A fitting that takes up the movement of a long PVC run as it heats and cools.
Fire-stopping
Approved material that seals openings through fire-rated walls and floors.
Hot-dip galvanising
Dipping finished steel in molten zinc for a thick, durable coating.
MEWP
Mobile elevating work platform, such as a scissor lift.
Permit to work
A written permission for work in a hazardous situation, with conditions.
Safe working load (SWL)
The most load per metre or per support that the maker allows.
Segregation
Keeping power cables apart from data and fire-alarm cables.
Snag list
A list of defects and unfinished items to correct before sign-off.
Space factor
The percentage of a trunking's or conduit's inside area that cables may fill.
Strut channel
Slotted steel channel used to make brackets, frames and trapeze hangers.
Take-off
A list of the quantities of each item read from the drawings.
Trapeze hanger
Strut channel hung from threaded rods, carrying tray or conduit.
UV-resistant
Made to withstand the sun's ultraviolet light without going brittle.

c1.title: Tray and ducts at a Falmouth hospital wing
c1.text: Kemar Ellis coordinates the installation of cable tray in a new hospital wing in Falmouth, Trelawny. The corridor ceiling void must also take an air-conditioning duct and a sprinkler main. The specification asks for ladder-type tray with supports at 1.5 m and fire-stopping where it crosses the ward walls. The drawings show the tray and the duct at the same height for 14 m. The crew's first bracket marks were made from an old drawing revision.

c2.title: An outdoor run at a Negril resort
c2.text: A resort at Negril, Westmoreland, wants cable tray and PVC conduit run outdoors along a sea-facing wall to garden lighting, over about 24 m. The plan shows aluminium tray bolted with copper-alloy brackets, ordinary PVC conduit and plain zinc-plated steel bolts. The wall is hollow concrete block. The resort is within 100 m of the sea and was damaged by a hurricane two years ago.

c3.title: Estimating a factory tray route in Spanish Town
c3.text: A factory in Spanish Town, St Catherine, needs 75 m of perforated tray along a roof truss for a new production line. Tray comes in 3 m lengths at J$7 800 each; allow 10% for waste. Supports are needed every 1.5 m with one at each end, at J$1 250 each with 2 anchors at J$130 each. The cables will weigh 22 kg per metre; the maker's safe working load at 1.5 m spacing is 30 kg per metre. A crew of 3 fits about 15 m each per day.

c4.title: Brackets at the wrong spacing in Portmore
c4.text: At a new school building in Portmore, St Catherine, crew member Andre has fixed 40 m of tray brackets at 2.5 m spacing, but the specification says 1.5 m. The tray is empty and looks level. Later the crew must also fix a busbar-adjacent run in the school's old electrical room, where the busbar trunking is still live and cannot be switched off during school hours.

questions.q: Before the crew fixes any more brackets, what should Kemar do first about the tray and the duct?
o: Bring the clash to the coordination meeting and agree routes
Fix the tray first, to claim the space before the duct arrives
Move the tray under the sprinkler main so they share supports
Ask the crew to leave the section out until the duct is in
questions.why: Clashes are settled on paper by the trades together, not by whoever fixes first. Agree routes, heights and clearances (the duct usually has priority because it is large and needs a fall), write it in the minutes and mark up the drawings. Sharing supports with another trade's pipe is not agreed practice.

questions.q: Why were the crew's first bracket marks a problem?
o: From a superseded drawing, so heights may be wrong
Marks on the ceiling slab are never accurate enough to use
Laser levels must not be used in a hospital building
Brackets can only be marked once the duct has been fixed
questions.why: Only the current drawings should be on site, with old revisions marked superseded. Setting out from an old revision can put the tray at the wrong height, causing a clash. Check the first brackets of each new run against the latest drawings and the minutes before the crew carries on.

questions.q: The tray crosses the walls between wards. What must be done where it passes through them?
o: Leave a gap around it so that air can circulate
Fill the gap with offcuts of cable and wrap it in tape
Seal the opening with an approved fire-stopping system
Cover the opening with a painted board on each side
questions.why: Fire-rated walls hold back fire and smoke. An opening must be sealed with a fire-stopping system, used as the maker's tested method says, and then checked and recorded. Gaps, offcuts, tape or boards do not restore the wall's fire rating.

questions.q: What is wrong with aluminium tray on copper-alloy brackets at this site?
o: Aluminium is too soft to carry any weight outdoors
In damp, salty air the metals corrode each other fast
Copper makes the tray conduct current along its length
The two metals are different colours, which looks untidy
questions.why: Where two different metals touch in damp, salty air they form a battery cell, and the aluminium corrodes fast (galvanic corrosion). Keep the metals apart, use compatible metals, or choose hot-dip galvanised or stainless steel throughout.

questions.q: Which finish and fixings best suit this sea-facing run?
o: Plain zinc-plated steel, painted after installation
Pre-galvanised tray with the cut edges left bare
Aluminium tray with fixings of plain mild steel
Hot-dip galvanised or stainless steel and fixings
questions.why: Close to the sea, plain or thinly coated steel and its fixings rust quickly. Hot-dip galvanised or stainless parts last far longer, and stainless fixings avoid weak points. Treat any cut or drilled edge, and avoid mixing metals.

questions.q: The PVC conduit is 24 m long in full sun. What must the installer allow for?
o: Shrinking as the wall dries out after the rainy season
The conduit sagging because the cables weigh too much
Movement as it heats and cools, so expansion couplings
Fading of its colour, which can be restored with paint
questions.why: PVC expands by about 0.06 mm per metre for each °C, so 24 m can change by about 40 mm or more through the day. Fit expansion couplings as the maker says and use saddles that let the conduit slide, and use UV-resistant PVC because ordinary PVC goes brittle in strong sun.

questions.q: The wall is hollow concrete block. Which is the best choice for the heavy tray brackets?
o: Ordinary expanding anchors, which grip any concrete well
Anchors for hollow block, or through-bolts
Plastic plugs and wood screws, since the load is small
Masonry nails, which can be driven in quickly
questions.why: In hollow cores an ordinary expanding anchor may have nothing to grip and can pull out. Use fixings made for hollow block, through-bolts or fix at solid parts, rated for the load and fitted as the maker says. After a hurricane this wall will be loaded by wind, so fixings must be secure.

questions.q: How many 3 m tray lengths should be ordered, with the 10% waste allowance?
questions.why: 75 ÷ 3 = 25 lengths. Adding 10% for waste gives 25 × 1.1 = 27.5, and you always round up when ordering, so order 28 lengths. Ordering 25 leaves no allowance for offcuts.

questions.q: How many supports are needed on the straight run, and how much do the supports cost before anchors?
o: 50 supports; J$62 500
75 supports; J$93 750
51 supports; J$63 750
49 supports; J$61 250
questions.why: 75 ÷ 1.5 = 50 spans, so 51 supports with one at each end. 51 × J$1 250 = J$63 750. Anchors, bends, labour and GCT are extra.

questions.q: The client later wants to add cables weighing a further 12 kg per metre on this tray. What should Kemar advise?
o: Not at this spacing: 34 kg per metre exceeds the 30 kg limit
Yes: the spare 8 kg per metre covers it, with margin to spare
Yes, if the extra cables are laid on top of the others
Yes, as long as the anchors are stainless steel
questions.why: The cables already weigh 22 kg/m; adding 12 kg/m makes 34 kg/m, above the 30 kg/m safe working load at 1.5 m spacing. Options are closer supports (which raise the SWL if the maker's data allows), a heavier tray or a second tray. Only the maker's data decides.

questions.q: How many days will the crew of 3 need for the 75 m run?
o: 5 days
3 days
2 days
9 days
questions.why: Output per day = 3 × 15 = 45 m. 75 ÷ 45 = 1.67, so the job needs 2 days (round up). Allow extra for access equipment, deliveries and other trades.

questions.q: What should Kemar do about Andre's brackets at 2.5 m spacing?
o: Accept them, because the tray is empty and looks level
Have the extra brackets fitted before cables go in
Use lighter cables so that the wider spacing is enough
Note it on the as-built drawing and say nothing more
questions.why: The specification and maker's data set the spacing for the load. Wider spacing means the loaded tray can sag or fail. Correct it now, before cables are installed, when it is cheap, and explain the reason to Andre. Recording it on the as-builts does not make it safe.

questions.q: The busbar trunking in the old room cannot be switched off during school hours. What is the best arrangement?
o: Work near it carefully and tell nobody, to avoid worry
Cover the busbar with a plastic sheet and carry on working
Work only at night, without a permit, when the school is quiet
A permit to work, with the busbar isolated and locked off
questions.why: Working near live busbars needs a permit to work and proper isolation: switch off, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester proved before and after, at an agreed time such as an out-of-hours shutdown. A plastic sheet gives no protection, and working in silence or at night without control is not a safe system.

questions.q: A 50 mm × 50 mm trunking will hold cables with a total area of 1 400 mm². With a 45% space factor, what is the position?
o: About 56% full: acceptable, as it is under 60%
About 28% full: acceptable, with room for more cables
About 45% full: exactly at the limit, so it is acceptable
About 56% full: too full, so use bigger trunking
questions.why: Inside area = 50 × 50 = 2 500 mm². The cables fill 1 400 ÷ 2 500 = 56%, above the 45% allowed. Overfilled trunking makes cables hard to draw in and traps heat, so use larger trunking or split the cables over two runs.

questions.q: A 40 m run of PVC conduit warms by 25 °C in the afternoon sun. About how much does it lengthen, at 0.06 mm per metre for each °C?
o: About 6 mm
About 60 mm
About 600 mm
About 0.6 mm
questions.why: Expansion = length × temperature rise × 0.06 mm = 40 × 25 × 0.06 = 60 mm. That much movement must be taken up by expansion couplings and sliding saddles, or the conduit buckles or pulls off its fixings.

questions.q: Which instrument should be used to look for hidden cables in a wall before marking and drilling the fixings?
o: A cable detector
A spirit level
A two-pole voltage tester
A continuity tester
questions.why: A cable detector (and pipe locator) senses hidden services behind the surface. A voltage tester only shows voltage where you touch it, so it cannot scan a wall, and drilling into an unseen live cable is a serious danger.

questions.q: Saddles hold a long PVC conduit run that has expansion couplings. How should they be fitted?
o: As tight as possible, so the run cannot move at all
Only at the couplings, leaving the rest of the run unsupported
Loose enough to slide, with one fixed point
Spaced twice as far apart as for steel conduit, to save time
questions.why: PVC must be free to expand and contract. Saddles are fitted to guide the conduit while letting it slide, with one fixed point between expansion couplings so the movement goes towards the couplings. A rigidly fixed run buckles or tears from its fixings.

questions.q: Two painted tray sections are joined with a bonding link. Why must the paint be removed from the contact surfaces and star washers used?
o: Paint is an insulator and would break the bonding path
Paint makes the tray expand more than clean metal does
Star washers stop the tray from rusting at the joint
Paint makes the joint look uneven once the link is tight
questions.why: Paint and dirt insulate. Bare metal to bare metal, with star washers that bite through any remaining coating, gives a low-resistance path so a fault current can trip the protective device. Test the result with a low-resistance ohmmeter.

questions.q: When is it right for Kemar to sign off a completed tray run so that the cable crew can start?
o: When every snag has been put right and checked again
When the crew say that the run looks finished to them
When the bracket count matches the number on the order
When the client has seen the run from the floor below
questions.why: Sign-off means the run meets the drawings and specification. Defects go on the snag list, each is fixed and rechecked, and only then does the coordinator sign. Cables should never be pulled on to a run that still has open defects.

questions.q: A crew fixing tray in a hot roof space at about 35 °C is working slowly and one worker feels dizzy. What is the best control for next time?
o: Longer shifts without breaks, so that the job ends sooner
Shaded breaks, water, and hard tasks early in the day
Working in the hottest part of the day to finish the roof space
Drinking a cold drink only when someone feels dizzy
questions.why: Heat stress is a real hazard in Jamaica's roof spaces. Plan shaded rest breaks, drinking water and heavy work for cooler hours, and watch for signs such as dizziness or confusion. Rest and cooling first for anyone affected.
